title: The Popular Revolution of Independence
author: Felipe Ávila
content:
_This article by[Felipe
Ávila](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Felipe%20%C3%81vila) originally
appeared in the [September 13, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/09/13/opinion/la-revolucion-
popular-de-independencia), Mexico's premier left-wing daily newspaper._

On September 16, 1810, the social revolution broke out from which Mexico would
be born as an independent, free, and sovereign country. On September 27, 1821,
independence was consummated, after an 11-year war that was a great popular
revolution to free itself from Spanish rule. It was a massive popular
revolution in which tens of thousands of men and women—Indigenous people,
mulattoes, mestizos, criollos, merchants, muleteers, ranchers, miners,
priests, and professionals—swelled the insurgent ranks, following the call of
Miguel Hidalgo, and formed a popular army that, in just a few months, dealt a
mortal blow to the colonial regime and dismantled an oppressive and
exclusionary social system.

The struggle led by Hidalgo and continued by Morelos was a libertarian and
justice-seeking movement, not only for independence and freedom, but also to
put an end to slavery and tributes, to a society divided into castes in which
a privileged few concentrated power and wealth, while the vast majority of
society lived in conditions of poverty and marginalization. It was a
revolution to end hunger and injustice, one that fought for a government and
laws that would promote a more just, free, and egalitarian society.

The social and libertarian content of the insurgent struggle was expressed
from Hidalgo's first decrees of October 1810 abolishing slavery and tributes,
as well as the concentration of land in few hands. It was proclaimed that all
should be able to enjoy the fruits of their labor and that oppression should
end; the struggle was waged against the exploitation of the haciendas and to
put an end to slavery in the fields and in the mines. That popular movement
also showed its rejection of the justice system that prevailed in favor of the
powerful.

The first phase of this process ended with the capture and death of Hidalgo,
Allende, Aldama, and other leaders. But the strength and legitimacy of the
insurgent revolution did not end with their deaths. Hidalgo's struggle was
taken up by José María Morelos, who, thanks to his political and military
genius, extended the revolution to the southern territories and convened the
Congress of Anáhuac, where he presented the _Sentimientos de la Nación_
(Sentiments of the Nation), a foundational document that captures the essence
of the liberating movement. In that text, Morelos established the bases of
what the new Mexican Nation should be, founded on popular sovereignty; the
constitution of a liberal government; as well as the establishment of laws
that would reduce poverty and inequality.

Article 12 of that founding text is not to be wasted: "That, since good law is
superior to every man, the laws our Congress dictates must be such that they
compel constancy and patriotism, moderate opulence and indigence, and in such
a way increase the wages of the poor that they improve their customs, driving
away ignorance, rapine, and theft." The same is true of Article 15: "That
slavery be proscribed forever, and likewise the distinction of castes, all
remaining equal, so that only vice and virtue shall distinguish one American
from another."

The insurgent struggle had an important participation of women. Josefa Ortiz,
Leona Vicario, Mariana Rodríguez, Carmen Camacho, Gertrudis Bocanegra, and
many more embodied the yearnings for justice and freedom that animated the
people and were fundamental to the triumph of the cause. These women took on
multiple tasks: convincing royalist soldiers to defect to the insurgents;
paying with their own money and jewels for the manufacture of rifles, cannons,
and bullets; supplying paper and ink for the newspapers; sending food and
clothing or helping the families of insurgents who had been killed or
imprisoned. Some of these brave women were captured, sentenced, and condemned
to confinement; several of them lost their lives.

The second stage ended with the execution by firing squad of Morelos. In that
phase, the movement reached the ideological and political maturity to
formulate the project of a free, independent, and sovereign Nation, with a
more egalitarian society and a government at the service of the people. Those
principles could not be defeated.

The third insurgent stage was one of resistance. With the armies of Hidalgo
and Morelos defeated, and their principal leaders dead, the liberating cause
was sustained as a guerrilla war. This resistance was led by Vicente Guerrero
in the south. Faced with the impossibility of defeating that resistance, and
after 11 years of civil war, a favorable juncture arose to bring it to an end
through the alliance between the royalist commander, Agustín de Iturbide, and
the insurgent commander, Vicente Guerrero, who decided to consummate
independence by means of a political pact that took shape in the Plan de
Iguala, with which practically all social groups and all regions identified.

With the Plan de Iguala, signed by most of the civil and military authorities
of New Spain, and the entry of the Army of the Three Guarantees into Mexico
City, independence was consummated and the free and sovereign Mexican Nation
emerged, with new institutions and laws that gave concrete form to the main
demands of the insurgent movement: the abolition of slavery and tributes,
popular sovereignty, freedom, and the equality of all before the law—demands
that were enshrined in the Political Constitution of 1824, which established
that Mexico would be a federal Republic. Thus concluded our independence, the
first popular revolution from which our Homeland was born.

_Director of the National Institute for Historical Studies of the Revolutions
of Mexico (INEHRM)._
